problems.title: Adding up the digits
problems.prompt: Complete the function `solution`, which returns the sum of the digits of the non-negative integer `n`.
hints: `n % 10` is the last digit, and `n // 10` is the number with the last digit removed.
Add the last digit and remove it, and repeat this until `n` becomes 0. If `n` is 0, the sum is 0 too.

hints: Remove the last digit one at a time, and count the digits that are equal to `d`.

problems.title: The day you exceed the goal
problems.prompt:
You have `start` followers today, and you gain `per_day` followers each day. Complete the function `solution`, which returns the first day on which you have more than `goal` followers.
Today is day 0. If you already have more than `goal` followers today, return 0.
hints: If you move ahead one day at a time and count the days until you have more than `goal` followers, you pass the correctness tests. A day with exactly `goal` followers does not count as more yet.
On day `d`, you have `start + per_day * d` followers. You can find the smallest `d` that makes this value greater than `goal` directly with division.
constraints: `start` and `goal` are integers from 0 to 1,000,000,000,000.
`per_day` is an integer from 1 to 1,000,000.

problems.title: Prime check
problems.prompt:
Complete the function `solution`, which returns `True` if the positive integer `n` is prime and `False` otherwise.
A prime number is a number greater than 1 that is divisible only by 1 and itself.
hints: 1 is not prime. Try dividing by numbers in order, starting from 2, and return `False` as soon as you find one that divides evenly.
If n = a × b, the smaller of a and b is at most √n. So you only need to try dividing while `i * i <= n`.
constraints: `n` is an integer from 1 to 1,000,000,000.

tests.label: Efficiency 3
tests.hint: Another prime close to one billion

tests.label: Efficiency 4
tests.hint: Large composite with no small divisor

problems.prompt: Complete the function `solution`, which returns how many primes there are among the positive integers from 1 to `limit`. `limit` itself is included.

problems.prompt: Complete the function `solution`, which returns the `k`-th smallest prime. The first prime is 2.
hints: You do not know how far you need to check, so use `while` to increase the number one at a time and count the primes.

problems.title: Finding divisors
problems.prompt: Complete the function `solution`, which returns a list of the divisors of the positive integer `n` in ascending order.
hints: If you divide by every number from 1 to `n` and keep the ones that divide evenly, you pass the correctness tests. `n` is a divisor too.
If `i` is a divisor, so is `n // i`. Increase `i` only up to √n and collect both divisors together. For a perfect square, do not add the same divisor twice.

problems.title: GCD and LCM
problems.prompt: You are given two positive integers `a` and `b`. Complete the function `solution`, which returns a list of their greatest common divisor (GCD) and least common multiple (LCM), in that order: [GCD, LCM].

problems.title: Sum of multiples of 3 or 5
problems.prompt:
Complete the function `solution`, which returns the sum of all the positive integers from 1 to `n` that are multiples of 3 or multiples of 5. `n` itself is included.
A number that is a multiple of both 3 and 5, such as 15, is added only once.
hints: If you loop from 1 to `n` and add each number that satisfies `i % 3 == 0 or i % 5 == 0`, you pass the correctness tests.

The multiples of `k` that are at most `n` are k, 2k, …, mk (`m = n // k`). Their sum is `k * m * (m + 1) // 2`. Add the sum of the multiples of 3 and the sum of the multiples of 5, then subtract the sum of the multiples of 15, which you added twice.
constraints: `n` is an integer from 1 to 1,000,000,000.

tests.label: Efficiency 2
tests.hint: Large n that is a multiple of 3

problems.title: Rice bags
problems.prompt:
You deliver exactly `n` kg of rice in 3 kg bags and 5 kg bags. You may use any number of each kind, including none of one kind. Complete the function `solution`, which returns the smallest number of bags you can use.
If you cannot make exactly `n` kg, return -1.
hints: The more 5 kg bags you use, the smaller the total number of bags.

Start with the largest number of 5 kg bags, `n // 5`, and reduce it by one each time. Find the first case where the remaining weight is divisible by 3. No matter how large `n` is, you find it within a few tries.
constraints: `n` is an integer from 1 to 1,000,000,000.

tests.label: Test 1
tests.hint: Small weight that cannot be made

tests.label: Test 2
tests.hint: Small weight that cannot be made

tests.label: Efficiency 3
tests.hint: Large n that needs two fewer 5 kg bags

problems.title: Second-highest score
problems.prompt:
Complete the function `solution`, which returns the second-highest score among the distinct scores in the list `scores`.
If the highest score appears several times, it is counted only once. If there is only one distinct score, return -1.
hints: Use two variables for the first-place score and the second-place score, and start both at -1. A score of 0 is possible too, so do not start them at 0.

If a new score is higher than first place, the old first place moves down to second place. If it is lower than first place and higher than second place, only second place changes. If it is equal to first place, change nothing.
constraints: The length of `scores` is from 1 to 1,000.
Each score is an integer from 0 to 100.

tests.label: Test 6
tests.hint: Ties for both first and second place

tests.label: Test 8
tests.hint: Later score between first and second place

problems.title: First and second place
problems.prompt:
You are given a list of student names `names` and a list of scores `scores`. The score of student `names[i]` is `scores[i]`.
Complete the function `solution`, which returns a list of the names of the first-place and second-place students, in that order. No two scores are the same.
hints: Go through the indexes with `for i in range(len(names))` and look at `names[i]` and `scores[i]` together. With `zip(names, scores)` from Python Basics §10.5, the code is shorter.
When first place changes, the old first place becomes second place. Move the score and the name together.
constraints: `names` and `scores` have the same length, which is from 2 to 1,000.
Each score is an integer from 0 to 1,000,000, and all scores are different.

problems.title: Rotating a list
problems.prompt:
Complete the function `solution`, which returns a new list made by rotating the list `nums` to the right by `k` positions.
Rotating by one position moves every value one position to the right, and the last value moves to the front. Do not change the original list `nums`.
hints: Rotating a list by its length brings it back to where it started. So you can rotate by `k % len(nums)` instead of `k`. An empty list has a length of 0, so you cannot divide by its length.
Rotating to the right by `k` positions is the same as moving the last `k` values to the front. If you make a new list with slices, the original list stays unchanged.
constraints: The length of `nums` is from 0 to 1,000.
`k` is an integer from 0 to 1,000,000,000.

tests.label: Test 9
tests.setup:
nums = [1, 2, 3]
solution(nums, 1)

tests.label: Efficiency 1
tests.setup: nums = list(range(1000))

problems.title: Range sums
problems.prompt:
You are given a list of integers `nums` and a list of ranges `queries`. Each element `[s, e]` of `queries` is the range from `nums[s]` to `nums[e]` (both ends included).
Complete the function `solution`, which finds the sum of each range and returns the sums in a list, in the same order as `queries`.
hints: Start the sum again from 0 for each range. Add the value at index `e` too.
Store the running sums from the front in a list `prefix` in advance. `prefix[i]` is the sum of the first `i` values. Then the sum of a range is simply `prefix[e + 1] - prefix[s]`.
constraints: The length of `nums` is from 1 to 1,000, and each element is an integer from -1,000 to 1,000.
The length of `queries` is from 1 to 1,000, and every range satisfies `0 <= s <= e < len(nums)`.

problems.title: Collecting hashtags
problems.prompt:
Complete the function `solution`, which returns a list of the hashtags in the post text `text`, in the order they appear.
A hashtag is a whole word that starts with # and is at least 2 characters long. Words are separated by a single space.
If the same hashtag appears more than once, include it only once, at the place where it first appears. Uppercase and lowercase letters are treated as different characters.
hints: Split the text into words with `text.split(" ")` and check them one by one. A word is a hashtag if its first character is # and its length is 2 or more.
Use `in` to check whether you have already added a tag, and add it only the first time it appears.
constraints: The length of `text` is from 1 to 1,000.
`text` consists of English letters, digits, #, and spaces. It does not start or end with a space, and there are never two or more spaces in a row.
A word that starts with # has no other # after the first character.

problems.prompt:
Complete the function `solution`, which returns a shortened form of the string `s`. Each run of the same character repeated in a row is written as the character followed by the number of times it repeats.

problems.title: Like and unlike
problems.prompt:
Posts are numbered from 0 to `n - 1`. `presses` holds the records of like-button presses in the order they happened. `[a, b]` means that person `a` pressed the like button on post `b`.
At first, every post has 0 likes. If the person who presses the button does not currently like that post, the post gains 1 like. If they currently like that post, their like is canceled and the post loses 1 like.
Complete the function `solution`, which returns a list of the number of likes left on each post after all the presses, in order from post 0 to post `n - 1`.
hints: Keep the pairs that currently have a like in a set, as tuples `(a, b)`. On each press, add the pair if it is not in the set, and remove it if it is.
First make a list of `n` like counts filled with 0. Add 1 when a like is made, and subtract 1 when it is canceled.
constraints: `n` is an integer from 1 to 100,000.
The length of `presses` is from 1 to 100,000.
The person number `a` is an integer from 0 to 1,000,000, and the post number `b` is an integer from 0 to `n - 1`.

tests.label: Test 10
tests.hint: Pairs that look the same when numbers are joined

tests.label: Test 13
tests.hint: Largest person number on a different post

problems.title: Matching brackets
problems.prompt:
The string `s` is made up only of parentheses `(`, `)` and square brackets `[`, `]`. The brackets match if each opening bracket is closed later by a closing bracket of the same shape, the pairs are properly nested, and no closing bracket appears without an opening bracket before it. Complete the function `solution`, which returns `True` if the brackets match and `False` otherwise.
For example, the brackets in `"([])"` match, but the brackets in `"([)]"` do not.
hints: Push each opening bracket onto a list used as a stack. When a closing bracket appears, check whether its shape matches the opening bracket you pushed last.
If the stack is empty when a closing bracket appears, or if anything is left on the stack after you read the whole string, the brackets do not match.
constraints: The length of `s` is from 1 to 100,000.

problems.title: Undo
problems.prompt:
`commands` holds, in order, the commands given to a text box. `"type"` followed by a space and a word (for example, `"type hi"`) adds the word to the end of the text, with no space before it. `"undo"` cancels one `type` command: the most recent one that has not been undone yet.
If there is no `type` command to undo, `undo` does nothing. Complete the function `solution`, which returns the text after all the commands are run.
hints: Push the words from `type` commands onto a list used as a stack. Then `undo` just means popping the last word you pushed.
In a `type` command `cmd`, get the word with `cmd[5:]` or `cmd.split(" ")[1]`. Popping from an empty list raises an `IndexError`.
constraints: The length of `commands` is from 1 to 1,000.
Each command is `"undo"`, or `"type"` followed by a space and a word. Each word is made of lowercase English letters, with a length from 1 to 10.

problems.title: Undo and redo
problems.prompt:
`commands` holds, in order, the commands given to a text box. The command `"type <word>"` (for example, `"type hi"`) adds the word to the end of the text, with no space before it. `"undo"` removes the most recently added word that is still in the text and sets it aside. `"redo"` takes the word that was set aside most recently and adds it back to the end of the text.
When a new `type` command is given, all the words set aside are thrown away. If there is no word to remove, `undo` does nothing, and if no word is set aside, `redo` does nothing. Complete the function `solution`, which returns the text after all the commands have been run. If the text is empty, return an empty string `""`.
hints: Keep the words in the text and the removed words on two separate lists used as stacks. `undo` pops a word from the first list and pushes it onto the second, and `redo` does the opposite.
When a `type` command comes, empty the list of removed words. Before popping, check that the list is not empty.
constraints: The length of `commands` is from 1 to 200,000.
Each command is `"undo"`, `"redo"`, or `"type"` followed by a space and a word. Each word is made of lowercase English letters, with a length from 1 to 10.

tests.label: Test 11
tests.hint: Removed word also appears earlier in the text

tests.label: Test 12
tests.hint: Undo and redo after typing again

tests.label: Efficiency 1
tests.setup: commands = ['type ' + 'abcdefghij'[:i % 10 + 1] for i in range(100000)] + ['undo', 'redo'] * 50000
tests.hint: 200,000 commands, undo and redo in turn after typing 100,000 words

tests.label: Efficiency 2
tests.setup: commands = ['type ' + 'abcdefghij'[:i % 10 + 1] for i in range(200000)]

problems.title: Matching format tags
problems.prompt:
`tokens` holds, in order, the formatting tags written in a post. `"<name>"` opens the format named `name`, and `"</name>"` closes it. A closing tag must have the same name as the most recently opened tag that is still open. A closing tag that appears when no tag is open also breaks this rule.
